chunks.text: Finding the area under a curve is one of the two great problems of calculus, since curved boundaries have no elementary area formula.
Riemann sums approximate the area under a curve by slicing the region into vertical strips and replacing each with a rectangle whose area can be computed.
For n equal subintervals on [a, b], each rectangle has width Δx = (b − a)/n.
A left Riemann sum uses the function value at the left endpoint of each subinterval as the rectangle height.
A right Riemann sum uses the right endpoint, and a midpoint Riemann sum uses the midpoint of each subinterval.
A Riemann sum is computed as the width times the sum of the heights: Δx times the sum of f at the chosen sample points.
For an increasing function, the left Riemann sum underestimates the area and the right Riemann sum overestimates it.
For a decreasing function, the left Riemann sum overestimates the area and the right Riemann sum underestimates it.
Over- or under-estimation can be determined by sketching the rectangles against the curve: rectangles poking above the curve overestimate, and those falling short underestimate.
Example: for f(x) = x² on [0, 2] with n = 4, the left sum is 1.75 and the right sum is 3.75, bracketing the exact area 8/3 ≈ 2.667.
The Trapezoidal Rule connects consecutive points with straight segments, approximating each strip as a trapezoid for a closer estimate.
The area of one trapezoid is its width times the average of its two endpoint heights: width × (f(left) + f(right))/2.
The trapezoidal estimate equals the average of the left and right Riemann sums.
A trapezoid overestimates where the curve is concave up and underestimates where the curve is concave down.
The Trapezoidal Rule works even when subintervals have unequal widths, making it the natural tool for tables of data measured at irregular intervals.
Example: with f at t = 0, 2, 5 equal to 4, 6, 10, the trapezoidal estimate is 2·(4+6)/2 + 3·(6+10)/2 = 10 + 24 = 34.
For n data points there are n − 1 subintervals when forming a Riemann sum or trapezoidal estimate.
When the integrand is a rate, the Riemann sum approximates the total accumulated quantity, with units of (rate units) times (input units).
As the number of rectangles approaches infinity and Δx approaches zero, the Riemann sum converges to the exact area under the curve.
The definite integral is defined as the limit of Riemann sums: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = lim (n→∞) of the sum of f(xᵢ)Δx.
The integral sign is an elongated S for 'sum,' and f(x) dx represents the area of an infinitely thin rectangle of height f(x) and width dx.
For a continuous function, left, right, and midpoint Riemann sums all converge to the same limit, the exact area.
